Sample text:
---
# The Moon Is Leaving

A total solar eclipse is a coincidence, and a temporary one.

The Sun is about four hundred times wider than the Moon, and about four hundred times farther away. Divide one by the other and the two disks come out the same size — close enough that, when they cross, the Moon can cover the Sun exactly, and the corona blooms into a black noon. Nothing in the laws of physics requires this match. It is a phase the solar system is passing through, and we happen to be awake for it.

The Moon is receding from Earth at about 3.8 centimeters a year. That is roughly the speed a fingernail grows. It sounds like nothing. Stretched across deep time, it is a departure.

We know because of mirrors. In 1969, and again in 1971, astronauts set out arrays of corner-cube reflectors on the Moon — boxes of mirrors angled to send light back along the path it came. Observatories on Earth still fire lasers at those coordinates. Nearly all the light is lost. A few photons return, a couple of seconds late, and from that returning handful we measure the distance to the Moon to within a few millimeters. The millimeters only add in one direction.

The bookkeeping is simple. Earth spins faster than the Moon orbits, and the Moon's gravity pulls the oceans into a bulge. Because the planet turns beneath it, the bulge is carried a little ahead of the Moon, and the bulge, having mass, tugs the Moon forward in its orbit. Forward means outward: the Moon climbs to a higher, slower orbit, and the payment comes out of Earth's spin. Angular momentum is only shuffled between them, never destroyed. Two cups, a fixed amount of water; as one rises the other must fall. Our days lengthen by about two thousandths of a second per century. The Moon, in exchange, rises.

Rewind. Four and a half billion years ago a body the size of Mars struck the young Earth, and the ring of molten wreckage closed into a Moon that formed close in — models suggest perhaps a sixteenth of its present distance, a Moon many times larger in the sky, hanging over a planet still reeling from the blow. Days may have lasted five or six hours. Tides would have been monstrous, walls of ocean sweeping inland twice in each short day, far past any shoreline we would recognize. Some origin-of-life stories put the first chemistry in those pools, alternately drowned and lit. We may owe our existence to a closer Moon's restlessness.

The rocks kept the ledger. Corals lay down daily growth bands, and Devonian corals some 400 million years old show about four hundred bands per year. The year was the same length; the days were shorter, around 21 or 22 hours. Time is a fossil.

Fast forward, and the match will not hold. Orbits are elliptical, so the coincidence is already fraying at the edges — some eclipses are already annular, the Moon a little too far, too small, a ring of fire instead of a covering. In roughly 600 million years the geometry fails for good: the Moon will be too small to cover the Sun from anywhere on Earth. Totality will be over. The corona will still be there, as it always is, but nothing in the daytime sky will make it visible. Whatever minds then look up will not see the Sun's atmosphere with their own eyes. They'll get rings.

The days will keep stretching. If the Sun were immortal, the shuffling would eventually finish: Earth's spin would slow until it matched the Moon's orbit, and the two bodies would lock, face to face — a day as long as forty-seven of ours, the Moon hanging fixed over one meridian, a lantern that no longer crosses the sky. The Moon already shows us a single face; it is locked, and the tides are the slow process of Earth being asked to return the courtesy. The Sun will not allow it. In about five billion years the Sun swells into a red giant, and the arithmetic of tides never gets to run to the end. The Moon will not finish leaving. The light goes out of the account first.

Which means we live in the sliver. For most of this planet's history the Moon has appeared larger than the Sun and covered it with room to spare. We live in the chapter where the two disks are nearly equal — the geometry at its most exact, totality at its most diamond-cut, the corona revealed like a thing unmasked. Whoever stands in the umbra today sees dusk in every direction at once, a 360-degree sunset, birds going to roost at noon. Our descendants, if there are any, will see a smaller Moon and will never stand in that dark. The coincidence has a run, and we are inside the run.

It is easy to think of the sky as the fixed part of the world, the one thing that holds still while everything below changes. Nothing up there is still. The constellations dissolve on a hundred-thousand-year timescale. The North Star is a job with a rotation. The Moon, the most constant thing in our sky, is a guest. Even the month is stretching beneath the word we got from it.

While it is here, it does quiet, enormous work. Its pull steadies the tilt of the Earth, which steadies the seasons. Its light times the mass spawning of corals and the hatchling dash of sea turtles. Its tides stirred the seas that may have been the cradle. We named the month after it, and a great deal of poetry besides. When it goes it will not exactly go. It recedes, which is a kind of leaving that never arrives at gone.

The part I like best is this: we have already begun to answer it. On clear nights, telescopes in Texas, New Mexico, and the south of France aim at the places where people stood, and wait. The round trip is about two and a half seconds. Of every pulse, a handful of photons make it home. The Moon is 384,400 kilometers away and opens that distance by the width of a fingernail every year, and still, when we call, a little of our light comes back.

It is leaving. It still answers.
---

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A lyrical science essay that turns precise astronomical explanation into a meditation on change, briefness, and connection.

## Grounded reading
The voice is lucid and patient, moving from measurements and physical mechanisms toward elegy without abandoning scientific detail. Its pathos comes from the contrast between immense timescales and our narrow chance to witness totality, then softens into a hopeful image of light sent to the Moon and returned. The reader is invited to feel both the loss in cosmic change and the tenderness of paying attention while something is still here.

## What the model chose to foreground
The essay foregrounds the Moon’s measurable departure, the temporary match that makes total eclipses possible, and the long exchange of motion between Earth and Moon. Mirrors, photons, coral growth bands, tides, and the eclipse’s “sliver” turn distant time into things that can be counted or seen. Its moral emphasis is not that change can be stopped, but that impermanence can make the present feel more vivid—and that even across great distances, something can answer.

## Evidence line
> The Moon is 384,400 kilometers away and opens that distance by the width of a fingernail every year, and still, when we call, a little of our light comes back.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The essay’s recurring movement from exact measurements to elegiac, human-scale meaning is coherent and distinctive, especially in its closing image of the Moon answering.
